title: Conflict De-escalation
blurb: Calming heated moments with your manner, listening and choices, and knowing when to step away and get help.
siteNotes: Who the duty manager is on each shift and how to reach them quickly
Where staff should withdraw to when a situation turns unsafe
legalNotes: From BHB-10MT-52. Advice is good practice on manner and listening; no statute is cited. 999 for a genuine threat of violence is as the trainer says.
See the conflict-lone-working session for how incidents are reported at the venue; this trainer does not cover reporting.

cards.title: Conflict De-escalation
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- keep your voice and body language calm and non-threatening
- listen, acknowledge and offer choices
- know when to withdraw and get help

cards.title: Take the heat out of the moment
cards.body:
Sometimes tempers flare, between guests or towards staff. De-escalation is taking the heat out of a moment before it becomes something worse.

Most of it comes down to how you carry yourself.

cards.title: Stay calm, keep it low
cards.body: Stay calm and keep your voice low, steady and unhurried. Shouting back or matching someone's aggression just pours fuel on the fire.

left.title: Do
items: Keep your voice low and steady

cards.title: Open and non-threatening
cards.body:
Keep your body language open and non-threatening.

> Never square up, point, or get in someone's face.

cards.title: Listen and acknowledge
cards.body: People often escalate because they feel unheard. Letting them speak, and saying something like "I hear you, let's sort this out", takes a lot of the heat out.

cards.title: Give choices, avoid ultimatums
cards.body: Avoid arguing, mocking or issuing ultimatums. Offer choices where you can. It gives the person a sense of control and a way to back down without losing face.

left.title: Do
items: Give them a way to back down

cards.title: Step away and get help
cards.body:
If someone is becoming violent or you feel unsafe, do not try to win. Withdraw, get help, and get a manager.

If there is a genuine threat of violence, call 999.

items.title: Withdraw and get a manager
items.text: Someone becoming violent, or you feel unsafe.

items.title: Calm, listen, give choices
items.text: Where it is still safe to talk.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Stay calm, with a low, steady, unhurried voice
- Keep body language open, with a respectful distance
- Listen, acknowledge and offer choices
- Do not argue, mock or issue ultimatums
- If unsafe, withdraw, get a manager, and call 999 for a genuine threat

cards.q: A guest is getting angry at the bar. To de-escalate, your voice should be:
options: Raised so they can hear you
Low, steady and unhurried
Quick, to get the matter closed
Light and jokey to change the mood
cards.why: A low, steady, unhurried voice helps. Shouting back pours fuel on the fire.

cards.q: People often escalate because they feel unheard.
cards.why: Letting them speak and acknowledging them takes a lot of the heat out.

cards.q: A guest is complaining loudly in reception. Which body language helps calm things?
options: Hands visible, relaxed stance, respectful distance
Arms folded and standing close to them
Pointing to show where you want them to go
Stepping in close so only they hear you
cards.why: Keep body language open and non-threatening: hands visible, relaxed stance, respectful distance. Never square up, point, or get in someone's face.

cards.q: Matching someone's aggression helps calm them down.
cards.why: Matching aggression just pours fuel on the fire.

options: Make them feel you are giving in to them
Give them a sense of control and a way to back down
Make them more annoyed that you are not listening
Show them that you have the final say
cards.why: Choices give a sense of control and a way to back down without losing face.

cards.q: You should avoid mocking or issuing ultimatums.
cards.why: Arguing, mocking and ultimatums make a person dig in.

cards.q: A guest threatens to hit a colleague. What should you do?
options: Stand your ground and out-talk them
Handle it quietly on your own first
Withdraw, get a manager, and call 999
Tell them to calm down and wait for them to cool off
cards.why: If there is a genuine threat of violence, withdraw, get help and a manager, and call 999.

cards.q: Winning the argument is more important than staying safe.
cards.why: If someone is becoming violent or you feel unsafe, do not try to win. Withdraw and get help.

cards.q: You say "I hear you, let's sort this out" to an upset guest. Acknowledging how someone feels tends to:
options: Take the heat out of it
Make it worse, as they feel patronised
Do nothing, as they are not listening
Give them a reason to ask for more
cards.why: People escalate when they feel unheard, so acknowledging them takes the heat out.

cards.q: Knowing your limits and when to get help is part of de-escalation.
cards.why: Staying calm, listening, giving space and choices, and knowing when to get help keeps everyone safe.
